'Then Michael, Uriel, Raphael, and Gabriel looked down from heaven and saw much blood being shed upon the earth' — the four-archangel intercession that responds to the cry of the oppressed. The four names establish the canonical Tewahedo angelology: Michael (warrior-defender), Uriel (light-bearer / scribe), Raphael (healer / binder of Azazel), Gabriel (messenger). Other Christian traditions know one or two of these; the Tewahedo Synaxarium honors all four with dedicated feast days, drawing the angelological framework directly from this Enochic chapter.

The archangels address the Most High: 'Lord of lords, God of gods, King of kings, and God of the ages, the throne of Thy glory standeth unto all the generations of the ages, and Thy name holy and glorious and blessed unto all the ages' — the foundational angelic doxology. The triple superlative (Lord of lords + God of gods + King of kings) becomes the Tewahedo liturgical model for naming God in the Anaphora prayers; 'King of kings' specifically (mèngèshte negus) becomes the Ethiopian imperial title (Negus Negesti = King of Kings) borrowed from this verse. The Tewahedo Anaphora of the Apostles preserves this Enochic doxology pattern verbatim.

1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36) (c. 200 BC)

'And they have gone to the daughters of men upon the earth, and have slept with the women, and have defiled themselves' — the archangels' formal indictment of the Watchers. The verb 'defiled themselves' (Geez 'irat) Tewahedo reads not merely as ritual impurity but as ontological self-degradation: the Watchers' descent into human sexuality reduces their angelic substance to a corrupted mixed-state. This grounds the Tewahedo monastic-ascetic theology of celibacy: not because sexuality is evil (Gen 1:28 stands) but because angelic-ranked existence has always been celibate by nature, and the monastic call is to anticipate that angelic mode of life.
